newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Australian journalist said still held in Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Australian journalist said still held in Malaysia.

text.p: An Australian journalist was still being held by police in Malaysia on Sunday morning after being detained on Saturday when a meeting East Timor activists was broken up, her husband said.
Nicholas Stuart told Reuters that Singapore-based Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) journalist Catherine McGrath was being held along with Malaysians detained after the meeting was broken up on.
The meeting, opposed by Malaysia's government, was disrupted when a youth group calling itself the Malaysian Action Front stormed into it shouting slogans and singing patriotic songs.
Police subsequently detained more than 100 activists, some of the youth group members, and at least two foreign journalists, including McGrath.
"It's just gone wrong," Stuart said. "They meant to arrest the people who'd come into the meeting, then someone made the decision everyone in there" should be picked up.

He said he had been in touch with Australian embassy officials and they were actively working to resolve the situation. He said so far as he knew no charge had yet been made against McGrath and he hoped she would be released on Sunday.
On Saturday a spokesman for ABC radio said McGrath had last contacted ABC when she had filed a story as she was being arrested.
The spokesman said McGrath told the radio station she had surrendered her passport to the Malaysian authorities at their request.
In Canberra, Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said the detention of McGrath and others by Malaysian police was unfortunate.
"This is a very unfortunate incident," Fischer said of the dententions in a television interview.
He had been asked if the detentions would affect relations between Australia and Malaysia.
Fischer said he had spoken to Australian diplomats in Malaysia and to Foreign Minister Alexander Downer about the incident. Downer had asked for a report, he added.
"We have taken consular action overnight. I have been speaking to the Kuala Lumpur High Commissioner Bill Farmer and also to Mr Downer. Minister Downer has called for a full report," Fischer said.
A Malaysian minister said last week that the government did not want the East Timor conference to take place because it could harm bilateral ties with Indonesia.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and now rules the territory in defiance of the United Nations.
Among those taken away by police on Saturday were two bishops, the Rev. Aloisuis Nobulo Somo of Japan and the Rev. Hilton Deakin of Melbourne, Australia.
The foreign participants in the meeting who were detained were expected to be deported, Malaysian officials said.
